faq.a: No – early NSTEMI may have a normal ECG; troponin and clinical judgment are essential.
faq.q: Can a normal ECG rule out ACS?

faq.a: Dual antiplatelet therapy reduces thrombus growth and improves outcomes after ACS.
faq.q: Why give both aspirin and clopidogrel?

faq.a: When primary PCI cannot be performed within 90 minutes and the patient presents within 12 hours of symptom onset.
faq.q: When is thrombolysis preferred over PCI?

exam: A 58‑year‑old diabetic presents with 30‑minute central chest pressure and ST‑elevation in leads II, III, aVF – what is the immediate next step and why? — Primary PCI if available within 90 min; otherwise give fibrinolysis because timely reperfusion saves myocardium.

A patient with suspected NSTEMI has a normal initial troponin. How should you proceed? — Repeat troponin at 3–6 h; if it rises, diagnose NSTEMI; meanwhile start aspirin and consider early invasive strategy based on risk scores.

Why is unfractionated heparin preferred over low‑molecular‑weight heparin in a centre without routine renal monitoring? — UFH can be titrated with aPTT and reversed with protamine, making it safer when renal function is uncertain.
What clinical feature helps you distinguish pericarditis from STEMI on ECG? — Diffuse ST‑elevation with PR‑segment depression, not limited to contiguous leads.

A patient with ACS develops hypotension and a new harsh holosystolic murmur. What complication should you suspect and what is the urgent management? — Papillary‑muscle rupture causing acute severe mitral regurgitation; urgent surgical consultation and afterload reduction.

In a low‑resource hospital without troponin, how would you confirm a diagnosis of NSTEMI? — Rely on typical chest pain, dynamic ECG changes, and bedside echo showing regional wall‑motion abnormality; arrange transfer for definitive testing if needed.

Explain why beta‑blockers are contraindicated in a patient presenting with acute decompensated heart failure secondary to ACS. — They reduce contractility and can worsen hypotension and pulmonary congestion.
List three modifiable risk factors that should be addressed at discharge to prevent recurrent ACS. — Smoking cessation, blood pressure control, lipid‑lowering therapy (statin).
ai.title: Acute Coronary Syndrome Presentation
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) is the umbrella term for myocardial ischaemia causing unstable angina, NSTEMI or STEMI. Recognising the pattern of chest pain, ECG changes and troponin rise guides urgent management, especially where resources are limited.

b: Unstable angina: chest pain at rest, no troponin rise.
NSTEMI: pain + troponin rise, no ST‑elevation.
STEMI: pain + ST‑elevation ≥1 mm in two contiguous leads.
sections.p: ACS includes any acute myocardial ischaemia with clinical evidence of myocardial injury. Diagnosis requires a compatible history, ECG changes and/or a rise/fall in cardiac troponin.

b: TIMI ≥ 4, GRACE ≥ 140 → consider immediate reperfusion.
Low‑risk (TIMI 0‑1) may be managed medically first.
sections.p: Risk stratification uses TIMI or GRACE scores; high‑risk patients need early invasive strategy.

b: Plaque rupture with thrombosis – most common.
Coronary spasm, especially with cocaine or herbal stimulants.
Coronary embolus – atrial fibrillation, rheumatic valvular disease.
Severe anaemia or sickle‑cell crisis increasing demand.
Infective triggers – malaria, HIV‑related vasculitis.
sections.p: Most ACS is due to atherosclerotic plaque rupture with thrombus formation. In low‑resource settings, consider additional triggers.

b: Chest pressure, diaphoresis, nausea, dyspnoea.
Silent ischaemia in diabetics – may present with dyspnoea alone.
Pain at rest or worsening night‑time angina.
sections.p: Typical pain is central, crushing, lasting >20 min, often radiating to left arm, jaw or back. Atypical presentations are common in women, diabetics and the elderly.
Use a stepwise approach: ECG first, then troponin, bedside echo if available, and basic labs.

t.b: Is there ST‑elevation, new LBBB or dynamic ST/T changes? → confirms STEMI or high‑risk NSTEMI.
Is there a rise/fall >20 % from baseline? → defines myocardial injury (NSTEMI).
Is there regional wall‑motion abnormality? → supports diagnosis, helps detect complications.

t.a: Full blood count, renal function, glucose
t.b: Identify anaemia, renal impairment, hyperglycaemia that affect management.

b: Cardiogenic shock – SBP < 90 mmHg, cool clammy skin.
Ventricular arrhythmias – sustained VT/VF.
Mechanical complications – papillary‑muscle rupture, ventricular septal defect.
Heart failure – pulmonary oedema, rales, raised JVP.
sections.p: Early identification of life‑threatening sequelae guides urgent therapy.

b: If PCI possible within 90 min for STEMI → primary PCI; otherwise give thrombolysis (streptokinase or tenecteplase) if fibrinolysis is the only option.
Heparin (unfractionated) – easy to monitor with aPTT; avoid LMWH if renal function unknown.
Beta‑blocker (IV metoprolol) once stable – reduces oxygen demand; avoid in bradycardia, asthma, shock.
Statin high‑intensity (atorvastatin) – start early for plaque stabilisation; if unavailable, use any statin.
Oxygen if SpO₂ < 90 %; nitrates for pain unless hypotensive.
Monitor vitals, ECG, urine output; treat complications promptly.
sections.p: Treat the thrombus, relieve ischaemia, and prevent further injury. Adapt to drug availability.

b: Lifestyle: smoking cessation, diet low in saturated fat, regular exercise.
Control hypertension, diabetes, HIV‑related dyslipidaemia.
Long‑term antiplatelet (aspirin + clopidogrel 12 months for ACS).
Statin therapy indefinitely.
Cardiac rehabilitation if resources allow.
sections.p: After the acute phase, secondary prevention and risk‑factor control are crucial.

b: Pulmonary embolism – pleuritic pain, tachycardia, S1Q3T3 pattern.
Aortic dissection – tearing back pain, widened mediastinum.
Pericarditis – diffuse ST‑elevation with PR depression.
Gastro‑oesophageal reflux – burning retrosternal pain, improves with antacids.
sections.p: Conditions that mimic chest pain or ECG changes.

b: Early troponin may be normal; repeat at 3‑6 h if suspicion persists.
ST‑elevation may be absent in posterior MI – look for reciprocal changes.
Anemia can blunt typical chest pain, leading to under‑recognition.
sections.p: Beware of false‑negative or misleading findings.

whenToSeekHelp: Chest pain with hypotension or shock
New loud murmur suggesting papillary‑muscle rupture
Rapidly worsening dyspnoea with pulmonary oedema
